title: Numbers One to Ten
label: ch:numbers-1-10
canDo: I can count from one to ten in German, say why every one of those numbers is the English number's twin rather than a Latin borrowing, and use ein and eine for "a".

payoff.summary: German's numbers are the one place the language is closer to English than any Romance language gets: they were never borrowed from Latin, they are German's own inherited words, and they are the near-twins of one to ten. This chapter teaches them one at a time, with the sound law that explains every difference between drei and three and between zehn and ten, and it collects each five into a run so that counting is one motion rather than ten remembered words. It closes with the article ein / eine, which is eins with its counting -s taken off exactly as English a and an are one worn down, and with the seam between words a language keeps and words it buys: the numbers are homegrown, the month names are Latin.
payoff.note: Chapter 6 is now generated from schema-v2 lessons, so the payoff is atom-scored rather than authored. It claims all ten number words, both counting runs, the article, and the four transferable rules -- that the counting -s drops before a noun, that a sound law is predictable rather than random, that German and English are siblings while Latin is a cousin, and that a language keeps its everyday words and buys its institutional ones. That is 17 of the chapter's 32 atoms. The per-number pronunciation and etymology atoms are drilled in their own lessons and are deliberately not claimed here: knowing that vier's v is said as an f is a lesson objective, not a test of whether the reader can count.
